subject: religious-studies
title: Hume's Quill: The Sceptic's Challenge
welcome_lead: Enter the Edinburgh study of David Hume, where every theistic argument faces the cool blade of empirical scepticism.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on Humean critiques of the design and cosmological arguments.
final_note: Hume reminds us that experience sets the limits of what we may claim to know.

concepts.def: Hume's posthumous 1779 work in which Cleanthes, Demea, and Philo debate the design argument.
Hume's objection that the universe is too unlike a machine to justify inference to a single, infinite designer.
Hume's revival of the idea that order could arise from chance arrangements of matter over infinite time.
Hume's distinction between relations of ideas (a priori, necessary) and matters of fact (a posteriori, contingent).
Hume's analysis of causation as merely the regular succession of events, not a necessary connection.
The 1948 BBC radio debate in which Bertrand Russell argued that the universe is 'just there' and needs no further cause.

walkthroughs.body_html:
In Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Philo argues that the universe more closely resembles an organism or vegetable than a machine, undermining Cleanthes' design analogy.

Hume also points out that we have observed only one universe, so we cannot generalise about its cause; and the world contains so much disorder and evil that any designer would be limited, finite, or perhaps a committee of gods.

Hume's analysis of causation in the Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748) reduces necessary connection to constant conjunction. We never observe causation, only one event following another.

This undercuts the cosmological argument: if we cannot establish necessary causal links within the universe, we certainly cannot infer a necessary cause beyond it.

In the 1948 BBC debate with Father Frederick Copleston, Bertrand Russell rejected the demand for an explanation of the universe as a whole. 'The universe is just there, and that's all.'

Russell accused Copleston of committing the fallacy of composition: just because every part of the universe has a cause does not mean the whole universe has a cause.
